title: Neural Network Backflow with Low-Rank Multi-Determinant Updates
authors: Tianshu Huang, Xiaowei Ou, Vidvuds Ozolins
abstract: Simulating strongly correlated fermions remains a long-standing challenge due to the exponential complexity of the Hilbert space and the intricate sign structure of many-body wavefunctions. We introduce a variational framework centered on a neural network backflow transformation that combines deep learning with variational Monte Carlo. The proposed ansatz employs a multi-determinant expansion with low-rank shifts to capture non-local correlations and complex sign structures. Applied to the two-dimensional Hubbard model at both half-filling and $1/8$ doping, the method achieves energies within $0.45\%$ of auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo at half-filling and captures intertwined charge- and spin-density stripe patterns at $1/8$ doping. These results demonstrate the potential of this framework as a scalable and interpretable approach to variational simulations of strongly correlated fermionic systems.
summary: This paper proposes a novel variational approach to simulate strongly correlated fermions, specifically using the 2D Hubbard model. It integrates a neural network backflow transformation with a low-rank multi-determinant ansatz within a VMC framework. This combination allows for scalable and accurate calculations, achieving benchmark energies while capturing complex physical phenomena like charge/spin ordering.
main_problem: Simulating strongly correlated fermions is challenging due to the exponential Hilbert space complexity and intricate wavefunction sign structures.
main_result: The method achieves variational energies for the 2D Hubbard model within 0.45% of AFQMC at half-filling and successfully captures charge/spin stripe patterns at 1/8 doping.
method: It introduces a variational framework combining deep learning with Variational Monte Carlo, using a neural network backflow transformation applied to a low-rank multi-determinant ansatz.
model_or_system: The primary system studied is the two-dimensional Hubbard model, characterized by nearest-neighbor hopping and on-site Coulomb repulsion U. The method is applied at both half-filling and 1/8 doping.
key_observables: Energy expectation value per site, relative error compared to AFQMC, and visualization of charge/spin density stripe patterns.
important_parameters: The ratio U/t (e.g., U/t=2 to U/t=8) and the doping level (half-filling vs. 1/8 doping).
main_assumptions: The use of low-rank factorization for determinant updates is crucial for maintaining computational efficiency and scalability.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow, from input embedding through the backflow network to the multi-determinant expansion. Figure 2 likely shows energy benchmarks on lattices of varying sizes.
paper_structure: The paper details the architecture, starting with the general variational framework, elaborating on the deep backflow transformation and its application to the multi-determinant wavefunction, and concluding with benchmarking results and discussions on computational scaling.
why_interesting: While focused on Hubbard models, the use of deep learning to parameterize complex many-body wavefunctions provides a powerful, generalizable tool for simulating strongly correlated quantum matter beyond traditional tensor network limitations.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic of the neural network architecture. (a) The overall workflow, where the lattice configuration x is processed through an input embedding and encoder to feed both the backflow network and the determinant expansion. (b) The Encoder architecture, featuring Nl layers of layer normalization, feed-forward blocks, and a static kernel projection α with residual connections to produce the encoded features xencoded. (c) The Backflow Network, which utilizes an electron feature projector and a spatial feature projector to generate mixed backflow coefficients F(x). (d) The Multi-Determinant Expansion block, where encoded features are spatially averaged and passed through a linear layer...

FIG. 2: Scaling of computational cost for direct determinant evaluation versus the low-rank lemma application with r = 2. (a) Training time per iteration as a function of the lattice sizes for a fixed nonzero shift counts (16, 16). (b) Training time per iteration relative to the nonzero shift counts (N∆M, N∆F ) for a fixed 4 × 16 lattice. Both plots utilize a logarithmic scale for the vertical axis.

FIG. 3: Variational energy per site for the 2D Hubbard model at half-filling with respect to different lattice sizes. The plot compares the performance of our deep backflow (Deep BF) to various neural network backflow architectures, including spin-block-separated (BW1) and spin-mixing (BW2) tensor backflow, both with one Lanczos step [41], and the auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) benchmarks [42] for different L × L lattice sizes. The Deep BF error bars are smaller than the markers.

FIG. 4: Relative error of the variational energy for the 8 × 8 Hubbard model at half-filling with respect to different U/t values. The relative error is calculated with respect to the AFQMC benchmarks [42].

FIG. 6: Variance extrapolation of the ground-state energy for the 4x8 lattice. The energy per site for the four network architectures (Net 1–4) is plotted against the local energy variance per site. The dashed gray line represents a linear fit to the data. The y-intercept indicates the extrapolated ground-state energy in the limit of zero variance, yielding Eextrap = −0.7681.
